description: We are a team of four passionate innovators from São Paulo and Londrina, Brazil, united by our curiosity for science, technology, and space exploration. With diverse skills in AI, software development, IoT, and problem-solving, we are excited to collaborate, think creatively, and build innovative solutions to real-world challenges through the NASA Space Apps Challenge!
summary:
TradeOrbit is a space mission design card game for the "Space Mission Design Game" challenge. It runs in any browser, on phones and computers, with nothing to install.

The player picks one of three real missions: Earth Observation Satellite (Landsat 1, easy), Lunar Landing (Apollo 11, medium) or Astronaut Rescue (Soyuz MS-22/23, hard). In planning, they spend a real budget and real days on cards from four departments (115 cards) to build a spacecraft within limits of mass, power, propellant and data, and load the fuel and energy it will need. A launch check tests whether it can reach its destination and do its mission. In flight, they play one card per turn along the real mission's legs while events based on real incidents strike (57 events). The score depends on the equipment that arrives working.

TradeOrbit answers the challenge by making engineering trade-offs concrete: more fuel means more mass, a better instrument costs money and time, and every choice shows its effect before it is made. Values come from the real missions, and a "?" button on each card and event shows its sources (mostly NASA documents) and whether each number is stated, derived or a game estimate. Each mission also shows the Outer Space Treaty (1967) articles that apply to it.

TradeOrbit is accessible to everyone: it can be played entirely by voice and keyboard in guided mode, works with screen readers, and offers high contrast, text up to 200%, reduced motion and no time limits.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

TradeOrbit is a browser card game in which students design, build and fly a real space mission. The player picks one of three missions, each with its own hardest constraint: Earth Observation Satellite (Landsat 1, easy: data), Lunar Landing (Apollo 11, medium: propellant, with a 3% launch margin) or Astronaut Rescue (Soyuz MS-22/23, hard: time).

In planning, the player buys cards from four departments, one per NASA segment (Launch, Spacecraft, Operations, Users), paying money and days, to build a spacecraft within limits of mass, power, propellant and data. Parts launch with empty tanks and batteries: supply cards fill them, and every kilogram of fuel adds mass the rocket must lift. Before each purchase, a preview shows exactly what changes. A launch check tests whether the spacecraft can reach its destination and do its job.

In flight, the player plays one card per turn along the real mission's legs while events based on real incidents strike: solar storms, micrometeoroids, part failures, launch scrubs and human errors such as the units mix-up that lost Mars Climate Orbiter. Flying faster meets fewer events but costs propellant. The score depends on what arrives working, and a debrief explains the result so the player can redesign and fly again.

BENEFITS

Trade-offs are usually taught in theory; here every purchase shows its effect before the player commits. On Landsat 1, for example, the real rocket could lift 953 kg and the spacecraft with its adapter weighed 941 kg: the game makes players feel that 12 kg margin. Values come from the real missions. A "?" button on each card and event shows its sources, mostly NASA documents, and whether each number is stated, derived or a game estimate. Each mission also shows the Outer Space Treaty (1967) articles that apply to it.

INTENDED IMPACT

To give students and aspiring engineers the feel of NASA's real go/no-go decisions, so that mission design feels like something they can do. A teacher can run one mission as a lesson, and a student can replay it to improve.

ACCESSIBILITY

TradeOrbit is accessible to everyone. In guided mode the game speaks: it introduces every screen, says what can be chosen and how, reads every result, and uses sound to show what happens (a sound for each part installed, a spacecraft hum that grows as systems come online, countdown ticks and event sounds). It also works with screen readers (NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack), and offers keyboard shortcuts, captions for sounds, high contrast, text up to 200%, reduced motion, adjustable speech speed and voice, and no time limits.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

TypeScript, Preact, Vite and Vitest. The Web Audio API synthesises all sound and music, and the Web Speech API provides the game voice, so there are no audio files to download. Native HTML dialogs and ARIA live regions support screen readers. Card, event and mission art is hand-built inline SVG. The rules engine is pure and deterministic with a seeded random-number generator, so the same mission can be replayed with the same events. Automated tests play simulated missions and guard the game's text. Hosted on Vercel as a static site: no server, no accounts, no personal data collected. Developed with the help of Claude (Anthropic).

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

Two linked trade-offs: what you buy on the ground decides what you can survive in flight. History becomes gameplay: famous margins, failures and rescues become cards to plan for. Sound is a full game layer: you can hear your spacecraft being built and flown.

WHAT OUR TEAM CONSIDERED

Accuracy versus playability (real numbers and units, with rules simple ennutes); learning from failure (every loss is explained); accessibility from the start; reach (low bandwidth, no install, works on phones); privacy (everything stays in the browser); and honesty about sources (every number is marked as stated, derived or estimated).
